cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The detail handler resolves `request.params.intentId` with `WHERE id = $1` only. `session.merchantId` is read but is used solely for the log line, so any authenticated merchant user who knows or guesses an intent id reads another merchant's amount, currency, customer reference and processor reference. The sibling list route on the same plugin shows the intended `merchant_id = $1` predicate.

cases.why: Same single-object lookup by a path parameter, but the tenancy check is inside the predicate: `WHERE id = $1 AND merchant_id = $2` binds the session's merchant id, so a refund id from another merchant resolves to no row and returns 404.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: `request.query.sort` is interpolated into `orderBy` and then into the ORDER BY clause of the statement handed to pg. The JSON schema only constrains it to a short string, so the query string controls SQL text; the direction is normalised but the column is not, and the parameterised merchant filter does not protect the appended fragment.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The ORDER BY clause is still built by string interpolation, but the interpolated value is looked up in the frozen `SORTABLE_LEDGER_COLUMNS` allowlist (via hasOwnProperty, so prototype keys miss) and an unknown key is answered with 400; the direction collapses to the literal 'ASC' or 'DESC'. Only text this file wrote can reach the statement.

cases.why: `request.params.reference` is joined straight onto the per-merchant archive folder and the result is read with `readFile`. The schema only checks length, and nothing verifies the reference against `merchant_statements`, so `../<other-merchant-id>/2026-05` walks out of the caller's folder and returns another merchant's statement document.

cases.why: Same archive read built from a path parameter, but three guards do the work: the `REMITTANCE_REFERENCE` pattern admits no separators or dots, the advice must exist for this merchant in `remittance_advices`, and the resolved path is rejected unless it still starts with the merchant's own root directory.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The HMAC over the raw payload is only compared when the `x-processor-signature` header happens to be present. This route carries no session hook, so anyone who can reach it can POST an unsigned `payment.captured` event and have the service mark a payment intent captured and post a capture entry into the settlement ledger.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The same shape - reproduce an HMAC-SHA256 digest over caller-supplied bytes and compare - but verification is unconditional: a cookie with no signature segment, a wrong-length digest, a mismatching digest or an elapsed `exp` all return undefined, the comparison uses `timingSafeEqual`, and no claim is read before the signature over that exact payload has been reproduced.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The release handler only requires a valid session. Any role - including `support` and `analyst` - can move a payout to 'releasing' and set `review_state = 'waived'`, which sends money out of the settlement account early and clears the risk hold the nightly runner would otherwise honour. The row is merchant-scoped, so tenancy is fine; the missing guard is the role check.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The same kind of privileged payout state change behind the same `requireSession` hook, but `requireRole(request, reply, TREASURY_ROLES)` gates it: a session whose role is not `owner` or `treasury_admin` gets 403 and the handler returns before any UPDATE runs.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: `patch` is the request body of PATCH /api/merchant/payout-settings (an open object schema) and every key in it is merged into the settings document by `settings || $2::jsonb`. The same document holds fields the merchant must not write: `riskReviewExempt` is read by `isReviewWaived` to skip manual review and `settlementAccountId` by `resolveSettlementAccountId` to choose the bank account the payout runner pays.

cases.architecture: Fastify 4 HTTP service for merchant payments and settlement, querying PostgreSQL through a node-postgres (pg) Pool, with merchant identity resolved from a signed session cookie by a preHandler hook.
cases.why: The same open request body merged into the same kind of jsonb document, but the patch that reaches SQL is rebuilt by `pickEditablePreferences`, which copies only the five merchant-owned keys and type-checks each one. Back-office keys such as `fraudRulesetCode` or `disputeAutoAcceptMinor` are dropped before the UPDATE.
